cells.tense: You are tending what is growing, and the tending is happening in the present.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're tending and give it one tending today, chosen for what it actually needs, not for what would look like progress.
cells.core:
There is something in front of you that hasn't decided what it's going to be yet, and you're giving it steady care anyway. Not because you know how it turns out — because tending it is the thing you do. Nothing is being forced. Nothing is being abandoned. You hold the order and the mess in the same hand, and it works.

The reason it works is that you're not clutching it. You're letting it take the shape it takes. Growth here means giving the care another day, which is not the same as effort — it's the willingness to keep showing up while it stays unfinished. One thing, today, chosen for what it actually needs.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what hasn't decided yet, and you don't force it.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with decisive care
cells.place: the open, undifferentiated potential before any choice has been made

cells.tense: You are bracing at a future you can't write into yet.
cells.ask: Let one thing stay unfinished today without touching it. Write down what you'd want to see finished, then close the note and do something else.
cells.core:
You're already spending on something that hasn't arrived. The care has sped up — checking, adjusting, planning the next move before the last one settled — and what was meant to keep it safe is starting to hold it too tight. You're not deciding what it becomes. You're deciding what it must become, and then watching to see if it does.

What you're doing is bracing. The bracing is spending the thing you want to grow. Vision here comes from having actually lived what's in front of you, not from imagining it finished. One thing, left alone today. Then something else, and let the note stay closed.
cells.sheetLine: You're forcing it toward a shape it hasn't chosen yet.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with decisive care

cells.tense: You keep standing at a door that is already behind you.
cells.ask: Name one thing you used to tend and haven't touched in a while. Spend ten minutes near it today without deciding whether it's alive or not.
cells.core:
Steady care looks like this. A thing gets what it needs, gets left room, turns out fine, and none of it exhausts the one giving it. The interest stays light. You can hold something a long while without gripping it, and that's ordinary here.

Distance is what's showing instead. You keep a step back from anything that hasn't proven itself yet, and a lot of what could have been tended hasn't been. Strength here comes from staying interested after everything that has happened. One thing you used to tend, ten minutes, today. Not to grow it back — just to be near it.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped tending it, and you're standing back.

cells.tense: You have the pen down in a room you are already writing in.
cells.ask: Say out loud what you've been holding for someone. Not how well you did it — just what you carried, in plain words.
cells.core:
You are tending something real — checking on it, making room for it, giving up other things to give it what it needs. And you describe it as just what's happening, as if the care belonged to the thing rather than to you. The care is running. The saying-so hasn't happened.

Seeing it named changes the weight. Someone says what they notice, and the carrying turns lighter for having been spoken to. What it costs, you pay. What isn't landing is that the cost is real and it's yours. One sentence, out loud: what you carried. That's the whole ask.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending it. You're calling it nothing.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with decisive care
